description: Passionate developer interested in Web Development, AI, Cybersecurity, and Space Technology. I love turning ideas into real, interactive solutions. For NASA Space Apps, I’m building an astronaut health monitoring platform combining AI, data visualization, and a modern UX. Looking for teammates skilled in AI/ML, Data Analysis, UI/UX, Space Science, and Presentation to build something innovative together.
summary:
ASTRA is a working web prototype for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.” It gives each astronaut a personal health record for heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood, and activity, then compares new readings with that person’s own reviewed baseline.

When values drift, trends appear, mood is very low, a reading is missing, or radiation is logged, ASTRA explains what changed, why the rule fired, how urgent it is, and what to do next. Cabin temperature and humidity sit beside the health record as habitat context, not as body vitals. Roles cover astronaut, medical officer, and administrator. The app works with manual logs, labeled mission scenarios, optional device telemetry, offline queuing, PDF reports, a local health copilot, and a 3D body explorer.

It is important because long missions put much of the first check on the crew, far from Earth clinics. ASTRA is decision-support and teaching software—not a medical device and not a diagnosis tool.
details:
What it does

ASTRA is an astronaut health-intelligence console. A crew member signs in, logs or receives health readings, and sees them next to a personal baseline. A rule engine (version 2026.1) reviews history and opens explained alerts for baseline deviation, trends, very low mood reports, missing measurements, multi-signal patterns, logged radiation context, and out-of-range quality checks. Levels are Normal, Monitor, Needs review, and Urgent review. Every alert shows what changed, why it fired, and a next step such as repeating a reading or contacting the mission medical officer.

How it works

Data enters through manual forms, a daily-routine checklist, seven labeled Mission Simulator scenarios, an offline browser queue that syncs later, and optional device ingest at POST /api/iot/telemetry. Measurements are stored in MySQL. Cabin temperature and humidity are kept as environment data and are never treated as body temperature. Radiation appears only when a value was stored, with unit and source. The same rule file can be reviewed in the browser. Live updates use Socket.IO after a stored packet or scenario.

Main screens

Mission dashboard, health intelligence, personal health twin, 3D body explorer, mission environment, daily routine, health copilot (local knowledge assistant unless an optional external API is configured), reports with on-screen and PDF output, references, administration and device registry, and a mission simulator.

Benefits and intended impact

ASTRA gives astronauts and medical officers one place to see personal change over time, with reasons attached to warnings, while keeping habitat context visible. It supports practice with rehearsable scenarios and remains usable when the link is slow through offline pages and a queued sync. Intended impact: better onboard decision-support and crew training for long-duration missions. It does not diagnose, prescribe, or replace flight surgeons.

Tools, languages, and software

Node.js 18+, Express, EJS, MySQL 8, Socket.IO, Chart.js, Three.js, PDFKit, Helmet, express-session, bcrypt, service worker + IndexedDB, Docker Compose for optional local MySQL, and a PowerPoint demo deck. Optional ESP32 / Wokwi-style device telemetry is supported for demonstration packets (not clinical sensors).

Creativity

ASTRA keeps source labels on every point, refuses to mix cabin air with body temperature, explains every alert in plain language, ranks urgency, supports three mission roles, and ties body regions and references to published NASA Human Research Program hazards and risks rather than inventing clinical claims.

Team considerations

We designed for distance from Earth, isolation and confinement, radiation context, hostile closed environments, privacy by role, honest labeling of simulated vs stored data, offline continuity, and clear non-medical-device boundaries on every screen.
